paragraphs.source_en: In the Saharan rock art most of the research has concentrated on descriptions of the art and on determining the styles and their distribution. Extensive records have been compiled, classifications elaborated and chronologies proposed, but very little has been done in terms of interpretation. The Round Head paintings have been described as "mysterious" since their discovery in the 1950s, but no author has dared to explore the possible meaning. This is mainly caused by the fact that this art has been studied by French and Italian scholars whose approach to the study of the rock art is purely technical. Such a method of study resulted in virtually every attempt at interpretation not only being criticised but also rejected.

paragraphs.source_en: The interpretation of the Round Head paintings is mainly hampered by the lack of ethnographic record. The mountains where these paintings are present are today very sporadically inhabited by Tuareg of Berber origin, believed to belong to a different ethnic group than the dark-skinned population who produced the Round Head images (Hachid 2000).

paragraphs.source_en: Due to the lack of any oral or written tradition directly regarding this art, an alternative way to approach the interpretation is to undertake comparative studies with other African rock art complexes. Studies of African religious beliefs and practices show that there are probably more similarities than differences (Mbiti 1969). Fundamental concepts like the belief in God and the existence of spirits and magic seem to have been retained when groups of people may have split or branched off in the course of the centuries, the new groups forming tribes recognised today as ethnic and linguistic groupings of African peoples. This may explain the fact that similar fundamental beliefs are found all over Africa, where names for God, words for spirits, rain, magic and medicine-men are comparable among many peoples.
